outcome: Given a human or nonhuman identity change, specify the approvals, provisioning or deprovisioning actions, downstream revocations, elevated-access controls, and evidence needed to keep permissions accurate.

sections.body: Provisioning creates or enables an identity and assigns only the access required for an approved role or task. A mover event changes duties, team, location, or project and should trigger both new approvals and removal of access no longer needed. A leaver event disables the identity, revokes sessions and credentials, recovers equipment, and propagates revocation to applications, cloud services, APIs, and physical controls. Automation helps, but an owner must verify exceptions and failed downstream actions.
keyPoints: Joiner, mover, and leaver events are business triggers that should be linked to access workflow.
Deprovisioning is more than deleting a directory object; credentials, tokens, sessions, keys, devices, and delegated access also matter.
Failed or delayed downstream revocation is a reportable control exception.
sections.title: Treat identity as a stateful lifecycle

sections.body: Role definitions should express business duties rather than convenience, and privilege escalation should be constrained, approved, time-bounded, logged, and reviewed. Just-in-time access can reduce standing privilege when the request, approval, duration, and action are attributable. Service accounts need named owners, narrow scopes, credential rotation, noninteractive-use controls, monitoring, and retirement conditions. Periodic and event-driven access reviews compare actual permissions to current duties and detect privilege creep, orphaned accounts, and toxic combinations of roles.
keyPoints: Least privilege includes removing permissions that are no longer required.
JIT access reduces standing privilege but does not replace approval, monitoring, or emergency governance.
Service identities require the same lifecycle discipline as human identities, adapted to deployment and rotation events.
sections.title: Control elevation, service identities, and review

sections.body: Review user, system, and service accounts against owner, business purpose, entitlement, activity, and risk. Provision and deprovision across onboarding, offboarding, and transfers must update authoritative sources, downstream systems, credentials, groups, sessions, assets, and evidence quickly enough for the consequence. Role definition and transition requires removal of incompatible old access as well as addition of new access. Privilege escalation through mechanisms such as sudo should be approved, scoped, time-bounded, logged, and reviewed. Service accounts need an owner, noninteractive purpose, least privilege, protected credentials, rotation, monitoring, and retirement. Typical abuse is orphaned access, standing admin rights, reused shared credentials, a transfer retaining incompatible access, or an unreviewed service principal outliving its application.
keyPoints: Make access decisions attributable to a subject, asset, action, context, owner, policy, enforcement point, and revocation path.
Test both expected allow behavior and abuse, failure, stale-access, or unavailable-dependency behavior.
sections.title: Control joiner, mover, leaver, privileged, and service identity states

summary: Identity access must change with the relationship, role, task, and risk of a person, device, or service. Joiner, mover, and leaver controls, privilege governance, service-account ownership, and recurring review prevent orphaned access and privilege creep.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.

Why this answer fails: “Reuse the original conclusion because the overall control family is unchanged” leaves the credential’s service dependency and accountable owner unresolved.
